old: This flexible body tissue once went by a homegrown English name before a French import muscled in.
Its ancestor is a Latin word, cartilāgō, borrowed into English by way of French.
The word it nudged aside, gristle, still shows up on your dinner plate.
clues: This kind of body tissue arrived from French and largely pushed aside an older native English word for the same stuff, though that older word still survives.
It is the firm but bendy tissue that shapes your outer ears and nose tip and cushions your joints, softer and more flexible than bone.
Sharks have whole skeletons made of it, and the older English word it partly replaced, gristle, now mostly names the chewy bits in meat.
